primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the truth' is understood first and foremost as the self-revelation of God in Jesus Christ — Christ himself is 'the truth' — and, by extension, God's word and the gospel message that reveals him. Knowing and abiding in this truth brings salvation and freedom, and it stands opposed to falsehood, deception, and the devil, who is 'the father of lies.' Thus 'truth' in Scripture is treated as personal and relational (embodied in Christ, communicated by the Spirit) rather than merely propositional accuracy.
primary_basis: John 14:6 — 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life'
John 1:14, 17 — the Word made flesh, 'full of grace and truth'; 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ'
John 8:31–32 — 'you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free'
John 17:17 — 'Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth'
John 18:37–38 — Jesus testifies to the truth; Pilate asks 'What is truth?'
John 16:13; 14:17; 15:26 — the Spirit of truth guides into all truth
Ephesians 1:13; Colossians 1:5 — 'the word of truth, the gospel'
2 Thessalonians 2:10–13 — being saved through 'love of the truth' / 'belief in the truth'
1 Timothy 2:4 — God desires all to 'come to the knowledge of the truth'
John 8:44 — the devil as liar and 'father of lies,' the antithesis of truth
Psalm 119:142, 160 — God's law/word as truth (Old Testament background)

alternatives.meaning: Christological reading: 'the truth' is Jesus Christ himself in person, not merely a body of teaching (John 14:6; Ephesians 4:21, 'the truth is in Jesus').
Truth as God's word / Scripture / the gospel message — the revealed content of Christian faith and sound doctrine ('the word of truth,' 'the pillar and buttress of the truth').
Pneumatological reading: truth as communicated and made effective by the Holy Spirit, the 'Spirit of truth' ('the Spirit is the truth,' 1 John 5:6); worship 'in spirit and truth.'

Truth as 'the faith' / orthodox doctrine — especially in the Pastoral Epistles, where 'the truth' functions almost as a title for the apostolic deposit of teaching, opposed to heresy; emphasized in creedal and confessional traditions.

Hebrew-background reading: truth (ʾemet) as God's faithfulness, reliability, and covenant steadfastness rather than abstract correctness — 'steadfast love and faithfulness' (chesed we-emet); prominent in Old Testament scholarship and biblical theology.
Ethical/behavioral reading: truth as integrity, honesty, and living/'walking in the truth' or 'doing the truth,' i.e., a way of life rather than a proposition.
Philosophical/apologetic reading: 'the truth' as objective, absolute reality grounded in God, deployed against relativism; common in modern evangelical apologetics though built on the same texts.
basis: Romans 1:18, 25 (exchanging the truth of God for a lie)

alternatives.meaning: Gnostic/esoteric reading (historical): truth as hidden divine knowledge (gnosis) accessible to initiates; rejected by orthodox Christianity but attested in early heterodox interpretation.
basis: Gospel of Philip and other Nag Hammadi texts (extra-biblical)

notes: There is a strong, recognizable consensus, though it is layered rather than singular: nearly all traditions agree that biblical 'truth' is ultimately personal — identified with Christ (John 14:6) and mediated by the Spirit and the word — while differing in emphasis. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions all affirm the Christological center; differences among the alternatives listed are mostly matters of emphasis (person vs. word vs. doctrine vs. covenant faithfulness vs. way of life) rather than mutually exclusive readings. The Johannine writings supply the bulk of proof texts, and John 8:32 and 14:6 are by far the most cited verses. 'Truth' is less a 'symbol' in the strict typological sense than a theologically loaded term, but its symbolic/theological identification with Christ and God's word is firmly settled in Christian interpretation.
